                    ### Question
                    A 39-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist for a routine visit. She has no complaints during this visit. She had an abnormal pap test 6 years ago that showed atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. The sample was negative for human papillomavirus. On her follow-up Pap test 3 years later, there was no abnormality. The latest pap test results show atypical glandular cells with reactive changes in the cervical epithelium. The gynecologist decides to perform a colposcopy, and some changes are noted in this study of the cervical epithelium. The biopsy shows dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Loop electrosurgical excision procedure
opb. Cold knife conization
opc. Follow-up pap smear in one year
opd. Follow-up pap smear in 3 years
ope. Repeat colposcopy in 6 months

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The presence of atypical glandular cells in the Pap test indicates a potential risk for cervical dysplasia or neoplasia. The subsequent biopsy confirming dysplastic changes necessitates intervention to prevent progression to cervical cancer. Current guidelines recommend excisional procedures for managing dysplastic changes, particularly when atypical glandular cells are involved. The Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure (LEEP) is a common and effective treatment option in this scenario, supported by the reasoning chains that emphasize the need for excisional treatment following biopsy confirmation of dysplasia. Cold knife conization is also an option but is less frequently used compared to LEEP. Therefore, the next best step in management for this patient is the Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure.
